title: EXPLORING EFFECTS OF LIGHTING IN PHYSICAL AND VIRTUAL SPACES
central_proposition: The paper proposes Human-Centric Virtual Lighting (HCVL) as a novel approach to optimize visual stimuli and enhance human-centered experiences in virtual spaces, extending the principles of Human-Centric Lighting (HCL) from physical environments.

concept_definitions.name: Light
concept_definitions.definition: Radiant energy that is capable of exciting the retina and producing a visual sensation in humans. The visible portion of the electromagnetic spectrum extends from about 380 to about 780 nanometers.

concept_definitions.name: Lighting
concept_definitions.definition: The application of light to a scene, objects, or their surroundings.

concept_definitions.name: Human-centric lighting (HCL)
concept_definitions.definition: Lighting that considers both the visual and non-visual effects of exposing humans to light and that widens the range of possible effects from visual performance and comfort to sleep quality, alertness, mood and behaviour with consequences for human health, learning and spending.

concept_definitions.name: Image Forming (IF) function
concept_definitions.definition: Neural processing of signals provided by the optic tract, which employs the optic nerve and chiasm and sends information to image formation structures that include the lateral geniculate nucleus (LGN), the intergeniculate leaflet (IGL), and the visual cortex of the occipital lobe.

concept_definitions.name: Non-Image Forming (NIF) function (or non-visual (NV) response)
concept_definitions.definition: Neural processing of signals via the retinohypothalamic tract (RHT) to the suprachiasmatic nuclei (SCN), which serve as a biological clock, and also serves other regulatory centers of the brain.

concept_definitions.name: Correlated Color Temperature (CCT)
concept_definitions.definition: The color temperature of white light is reported as Correlated Color Temperature (CCT) in Kelvin (K).

concept_definitions.name: Conceptual lighting
concept_definitions.definition: Implicit expectations about lighting for a given environment, where physical lighting parameters match or mismatch these expectations.

concept_definitions.name: Human-centric virtual lighting (HCVL)
concept_definitions.definition: An adaptation of HCL for virtual spaces, aiming to integrate both visual and non-visual effects of virtual lighting to produce physiological and/or psychological benefits upon humans.

argument_structure: The paper first reviews the current state of lighting research in physical spaces, including definitions, parameters, effects in various contexts, and research methods (Part I). It identifies research gaps, particularly regarding non-visual effects and virtual spaces. Then, it presents empirical studies on CCT effects on conflict handling in physical spaces (Part II) and lighting effects on perception and quality of stay in virtual spaces (Part III). Finally, it synthesizes these findings to propose a Human-Centric Virtual Lighting (HCVL) approach and partial models, discussing practical implications and future research directions.
mechanism_or_causal_logic: The core causal logic revolves around the dual effects of light: (1) Visual effects (Image Forming - IF) relate to how light enables perception of objects, colors, brightness, and spatial patterns, influencing subjective appraisal. (2) Non-visual effects (Non-Image Forming - NIF) describe how light's spectral composition (e.g., blue light) influences physiological processes (e.g., melatonin suppression, circadian rhythms, arousal) and psychological states (e.g., alertness, mood, cognitive performance). (3) Conceptual Lighting posits that repeated exposure to certain lighting conditions in specific environments creates implicit associations, where incongruence with these expectations can lead to psychological effects. (4) The paper argues that these IF, NIF, and conceptual lighting mechanisms are transferable to virtual environments, influencing user perception, emotional states, and quality of stay, despite technical limitations of displays.

testable_hypotheses_or_predictions: High CCT values of virtual lighting will be associated with a higher evaluation of spaciousness in future trials.
A stimulating effect in virtual environments can be promoted using high CCT lighting scenarios and virtual daylight, useful for education or business applications.
In virtual trainings, users will remain more attentive, awake, and concentrated with stimulating visual stimuli.
Counter-conceptual lighting in virtual spaces may lead to an avoiding conflict handling style.
Virtual houses will incorporate windows with a view to the virtual outside world, even if not technically necessary.
bridge_warrants: The results of the virtual lighting exploration are consistent with findings from previous investigations of physical spaces, suggesting transferability of effects.
The findings from virtual lighting studies coincide with findings from studies of physical spaces regarding visual and non-visual effects.

The plausibility of HCVL results is reviewed against current literature, indicating its potential to optimize visual stimuli and enhance human-centered experiences in virtual spaces, similar to HCL in physical spaces.
Established measurement methods from physical illumination and perception research can be applied in virtual environments.
methodological_critiques: Absence of a standardized investigation approach in lighting research.
Technical capabilities of devices (HMDs, monitors) limit the reproduction of glare and luminous stimuli in virtual environments.
Lack of standardization in measurement instruments, with semantic differential scales differing in level, polarity, and number of items.
Difficulty in assessing the most suitable scaling method (e.g., 7-point vs. 9-point scales).
Need for clear definitions and explanations of constructs and scales to avoid scoring inaccuracies.
Heterogeneity in technical specifications of devices (brightness, resolution, color rendering) in biotic studies can confound results.
Displaying static screenshots instead of allowing movement in virtual environments may limit subjective ratings.
Actual properties of daylight (brightness, spectral distribution) can only be reproduced to a limited extent due to display technical limitations.
Heterogeneous participant samples (age, sex, nationality) in biotic studies may introduce confounding effects.
Interindividual variability (e.g., genetic polymorphisms, biological sex) is an important factor in determining circadian effects.
Lack of physiological measurements (e.g., heart rate, skin resistance) limits the examination of somatic effects of lighting.
Complex constructs like conflict behavior are stable and not easily influenced by lighting conditions as a sole environmental factor.
Simplified causal relationships between light and immediate behavior (apart from endocrinological effects) should be critically examined.
Uncontrollable confounding variables and multimodal sensory influences in biotic environments can affect evaluations.
Technical deviations in monitor production batches or lifetime can occur, even with identical models.
Other inter- and intrapersonal variables (fatigue, hunger, emotional states) can influence assessments.
model_structure: The paper proposes a Human-Centric Virtual Lighting (HCVL) approach, which is an initial framework for designing lighting in virtual spaces. This approach is structured into three main inputs: CCT condition, Daylight condition, and General preferences. These inputs are theorized to influence various visual and non-visual effects, which are categorized by semantic differentials (e.g., 'Confined – spacious', 'Visually warm – visually cold', 'Bright – dim'). Two partial HCVL models are presented: one for CCT conditions and one for virtual daylight, detailing specific semantic differentials and their associated effect sizes (Pearson's r) derived from empirical studies. General preferences for virtual spaces (e.g., open sky, realistic lighting, sunny sky) are also integrated into the overall HCVL approach.
limitations: The physical space experiments were conducted between 2017-2019, preceding the full development of standardized lighting study guidelines, potentially affecting comparability with newer research.
The wall color of the laboratory environment (black) in Studies CH1 and CH2 deviates from current recommendations (solid white) for comparability.
Continuous technical progress in virtual reality software and hardware necessitates ongoing research to keep HCVL models current.
Non-image forming effects of lighting are difficult to transfer to complex behavioral constructs like conflict handling.
The direct causal influence of lighting as a sole determinant of complex behaviors must be critically evaluated.
The HCVL approach is an initial framework, not a mathematically exact calculation, representing probable effects rather than precise predictions.
General preferences for virtual lighting may vary significantly across specific contexts (e.g., gaming, business, education), requiring further context-dependent studies.
The study's sample for VL2 (undergraduate students aged 18-26) limits generalizability to a broader population.
Movement through virtual spaces introduces additional complexity not fully addressed in studies using static screenshots.
The biotic environment of VL1 introduced uncontrollable confounding variables and potential multisensory influences.
Technical limitations of displays restrict the accurate reproduction of daylight properties (brightness, spectral distribution).
Heterogeneity in participant demographics (age, sex, nationality) in VL1 may have influenced results.
The current state of lighting research, particularly for virtual environments, is incomplete and not yet sufficiently applied to practice.

theory_commitments.specific_claim: A conceptual framework is proposed to integrate and explain the effects of lighting characteristics (e.g., Correlated Color Temperature) on human perception and experience in both physical and virtual environments.
Basic principles of environmental perception and human response to environmental cues are assumed to apply across physical and virtual contexts.
